vision.oneLine: Ind AS 115 tells you when and how much revenue to recognise from contracts with customers, through one five-step model.
vision.why: Revenue is the most important number in any income statement, and Ind AS 115 is examined in every FR attempt: 5–20 marks in each question paper since May 2022, plus case-scenario MCQs. It also links to ethics (premature revenue in a CA's professional duty case), Ind AS 109 (receivables, financing), Ind AS 116 (repurchase as lease) and Ind AS 37 (warranties, onerous contracts).
vision.marks: about 9 marks an attempt (5–20 in papers since May 2022)
sixty: Revenue = transfer of promised goods/services, at the amount you expect to be entitled to.
Step 1: enforceable contract — five criteria, collection probable.
Step 2: split into distinct promises; options with a material right are promises too.
Step 3: price = fixed + constrained variable ± financing + non-cash − payable to customer.
Step 4: share the price on stand-alone selling prices; discounts go to a bundle only with evidence.
Step 5: over time if consumed as you go, customer controls WIP, or no alternative use + right to payment; else at a point in time.
Special cases: returns, warranties, repurchase, bill-and-hold, licences, royalties.
Costs: capitalise incremental costs to obtain and qualifying fulfilment costs.

askedAs.how: A fact pattern ending "Determine how revenue will be recognised" — bill-and-hold, loyalty points, modifications, financing, SCA.
2-mark MCQs on allocation (vouchers), progress, returns, barter and modifications inside a mixed case.
Premature revenue recognition judged against Ind AS 115 and the CA's professional duty (RTP May 2024, RTP Nov 2026, MTP Sep 2025).
SM PQ 8, 9 and 10 have reappeared verbatim in RTPs; Illustrations 23, 65 and 68 return with new figures.

pitfalls: Using the full voucher discount instead of the incremental discount.
Including uninstalled materials in the measure of progress.
Forgetting the "highly probable" constraint sentence on bonuses.
Netting the refund liability against the return asset.
Recognising the whole promised amount when payment is deferred beyond a year.
Calling a licence "over time" because it is paid monthly.

levels.title: The core principle and the five steps
levels.hook: Every Ind AS 115 answer is written by walking the five steps — examiners give marks step by step.

teach.html: Recognise revenue to show the transfer of promised goods or services at the amount the entity expects to be entitled to.

• 1 Identify the contract
  • 2 Identify the performance obligations
  • 3 Determine the transaction price
  • 4 Allocate it to the performance obligations
  • 5 Recognise revenue when (or as) control transfers

Leases (Ind AS 116), insurance (Ind AS 117), financial instruments and interests in other entities (Ind AS 109/110/111/27/28), and non-monetary exchanges between entities in the same line of business to facilitate sales. Barter of dissimilar services (talk time for power) is in scope.

levels.picture:
StepQuestion you ask
1Is there an enforceable contract?
2What distinct things did we promise?
3How much do we expect to get?
4How much belongs to each promise?
5When does the customer get control?

recall.q: Put the five steps in order.
recall.why: Contract first: it is the gateway to the other four.

recall.q: Two oil companies swapping oil to meet each other's customers' demand is within Ind AS 115.
recall.why: Excluded: a non-monetary exchange between entities in the same line of business to facilitate sales (para 5(d)).

recall.q: A telecom company gives 1,00,000 minutes of talk time (₹0.50 a minute) to a power company in exchange for 20,000 units of power (₹2.5 a unit). Revenue of the telecom company?
recall.why: Dissimilar exchange → in scope; measure non-cash consideration at fair value: 20,000 × ₹2.5 = ₹50,000 (SM TYK 2).

twist.q: What if both companies sold identical goods and swapped them to serve customers in other cities?
twist.a: Then it is a same-line-of-business exchange to facilitate sales — outside Ind AS 115, no revenue.

levels.title: Step 1 — does a contract exist, and for how long?
levels.hook: Collectability and termination rights are favourite one-paragraph theory questions.

teach.html: Approved and committed; rights identifiable; payment terms identifiable; commercial substance; probable (more likely than not) collection of what the entity expects to be entitled to.

Consideration received is a liability until the criteria are met, or the entity has no remaining obligations and has received substantially all non-refundable consideration, or the contract is terminated and the amount is non-refundable (paras 15–16).

Account only for the period with enforceable rights: a 12-month gym membership cancellable without penalty after 3 months is a 3-month contract. Combine contracts with the same customer (or its related parties) at or near the same time if negotiated as a package, prices are inter-dependent, or they form one performance obligation.

levels.correlate: Collectability looks at the amount the entity expects — after any expected price concession. That is why SM TYK 5 tests ₹1.75 million, not ₹2 million.

recall.q: G Ltd. sells machinery for ₹20 lakh; the buyer pays ₹1 lakh and the rest on non-recourse finance out of a risky new business. How does G Ltd. treat the ₹1 lakh?
opts: Deposit liability until the para 9 criteria are met or a para 15 event occurs
recall.why: Collection is not probable, so no contract exists for Ind AS 115; the deposit is a liability (SM TYK 4).

recall.q: A gym contract is 12 months at ₹4,500 a month, cancellable without penalty after 3 months. Contract term in months?
recall.why: Enforceable rights exist only for 3 months (SM Illustration 2).

recall.q: Two contracts with the same government's two entities, signed a week apart with a deep discount only if both buy, should be combined.
recall.why: Related parties, near the same time, single package and inter-dependent price (SM Illustration 6).

twist.q: The gym member would pay a substantive penalty for cancelling at any time in the year. Term?
twist.a: 12 months — a substantive termination penalty is evidence of enforceable rights for the whole period it covers.

levels.title: Contract modifications
levels.hook: Asked in nearly every attempt as PQ 8 or a variant: bonus constrained, then modification with catch-up.

teach.html:
• Separate contract: distinct goods added at their stand-alone price.
  • Terminate and start again (prospective): remaining goods distinct.
  • Cumulative catch-up: remaining goods not distinct, part of one partly satisfied obligation.

Blend the price: (original + added) ÷ revised total units; re-book work done at the blended rate; the difference hits revenue now. SM Illustration 9: ₹35,000 ÷ 250 = ₹140; 100 × ₹140 − ₹15,000 = ₹(1,000).

levels.picture:
Remaining goods/servicesTreatment
Distinct + priced at SSPSeparate contract
DistinctProspective (new contract)
Not distinctCumulative catch-up

recall.q: 200 hours at ₹300; after 100 hours, 50 more hours added at ₹200. Cumulative catch-up adjustment (₹)?
30 extra products at ₹950 (their stand-alone price) are added to a 120-unit order at ₹1,000. Treatment?
opts: Prospective re-allocation of the whole contract
recall.why: Distinct goods at stand-alone price → separate contract (SM Illustration 7).

recall.q: A retention credit the customer did not expect, given in month 14, is variable consideration.
recall.why: It is a change in price accounted for as a contract modification over the remaining term (SM Illustration 58).

twist.q: In PQ 8, the modification also extends the bonus deadline so the bonus becomes highly probable. What changes?
twist.a: Include the ₹2,50,000 bonus in the transaction price with the modification and re-run the catch-up: 60.60% × ₹24,00,000 − ₹13,00,000 = ₹1,54,400.

levels.title: Step 2 — distinct performance obligations and series
levels.hook: Case scenarios love bundles: software + installation + updates, telecom + modem, property + golf membership.

teach.html: Capable of being distinct (benefit alone or with readily available resources) and distinct in the context of the contract (no significant integration, modification/customisation or high interdependence).
Customary practice, published policies or advertising can create performance obligations (free maintenance advertised by a carmaker; free support to a reseller's customers).
Distinct services that are substantially the same and transfer over time with the same progress measure are one performance obligation — mandatory (cleaning, payroll, hotel management).

levels.picture:
BundlePerformance obligations
Water purification plant with integration1
Broadband + voice + modem3
Licence + installation + updates + support4
Same, but installation significantly customises3
Anti-virus licence + critical updates1

recall.q: Software licence, installation (routine, others can do it), unspecified updates and two-year support. How many performance obligations?
recall.why: Each is distinct (SM Illustration 15).

recall.q: A telecom activation fee is a separate performance obligation.
recall.why: Activation transfers nothing to the customer; the fee is an advance for the data service (SM Illustration 28).

recall.q: In a property sale, which item is LIKELY to be a separate performance obligation?
opts: Undivided interest in land in an apartment block
recall.why: Property management and golf membership can be used alone and are not integrated with the property (SM PQ 6).

twist.q: In the software contract the installation now adds significant new functionality to interface with other systems. How many performance obligations?
twist.a: Three: customised installation including the licence (one), updates, support (SM Illustration 16).

levels.title: Customer options, loyalty points, principal vs agent, consignment
levels.hook: Material rights are the single most-asked Ind AS 115 topic in the 2022–26 papers.

teach.html: An option is a separate performance obligation only if it gives a discount the customer would not get without the contract. Price it: expected spend × incremental discount × likelihood of use; then allocate on relative SSPs.

Defer points at sale: Sale × points value ÷ (sale + points value), where points value reflects expected redemption. Release as points are redeemed: deferred × redeemed to date ÷ total expected − released earlier.
Does the entity control the good or service before transfer? Indicators: primary responsibility, inventory risk, pricing discretion. Principal → gross; agent → net commission.

levels.correlate: Points redeemable with a partner bring in principal vs agent; consignment differs from a right of return because the consignee never gets control.

recall.q: Sale ₹1,000 with a 40% voucher; everyone gets 10% anyway; 80% likely to be used on ₹500 of purchases. Allocated to the voucher (₹, nearest 10)?
100 points (SSP ₹500) earned on a ₹10,000 stay. Allocated to points (₹)?
A travel entity buys tickets in advance, bears unsold-ticket risk and sets resale prices. It is…
opts: An agent because the airline flies the plane
recall.why: It controls the ticket (right to fly) before transfer (SM Illustration 26).

twist.q: Seasonal discount for everyone rises from 10% to 40%. Is the voucher still a material right?
twist.a: No — it gives no discount beyond what any customer gets; it is a marketing offer accounted for only when used.

levels.title: Step 3 — variable consideration, the constraint, returns and warranties
levels.hook: Numerical heavyweights: volume tiers, returns and bonuses appear in RTPs, MTPs and papers.

teach.html: Expected value for a range; most likely amount for two outcomes. One method per uncertainty, applied consistently.
Include only what is highly probable not to reverse significantly — think market-linked fees, long uncertainty, little experience, broad concessions.

Return right: revenue on units kept, refund liability, asset for goods coming back at cost. Warranty you can buy separately (or service beyond assurance) → performance obligation; basic assurance → Ind AS 37 provision.

levels.picture:
SituationMethod
Bonus 15%/10%/5%/0% with probabilitiesExpected value
Bonus earned or notMost likely
Fee linked to market index over 5 yearsConstrained to nil

recall.q: 1,000 products at ₹50, cost ₹30, 970 expected to be kept. Refund liability (₹)?
recall.why: 30 × ₹50 = 1,500; revenue 48,500; asset 30 × ₹30 = 900 (SM Illustration 34).

recall.q: Volume tiers: estimate 2.8 million containers → ₹90; 7,00,000 sold at ₹100 in Q1. Liability (₹ million)?
recall.why: 7,00,000 × ₹10 = ₹7 million; revenue ₹63 million (SM TYK 6).

recall.q: Computer ₹36,000 with an extended warranty sold separately (SSPs ₹32,000 / ₹4,000) and 90-day assurance cost ₹2,000. Revenue on sale?
recall.why: ₹4,000 is a contract liability; ₹2,000 is a warranty provision (SM Illustration 35).

twist.q: The product is new and there is no evidence of returns. What happens to revenue at delivery?
twist.a: The constraint may stop any revenue being recognised until the return period ends (SM Illustration 38).

levels.title: Financing, non-cash consideration and amounts payable to customers
levels.hook: Financing questions recur in RTP Nov 2024 and the 2022–26 papers with a twist on the discount rate.

teach.html: Revenue at the cash selling price; interest separately, at the rate of a separate financing transaction (not updated later). No adjustment if the gap is ≤ 1 year, the customer controls timing of prepaid services, a royalty drives the amount, or the gap is for protection (retention money).
Fair value at inception; later changes due to the form (share price) ignored; changes due to performance are variable consideration.
Slotting fees, shelving payments, port-in credits reduce the price — unless paid for a distinct good or service at fair value.

recall.q: ₹1,21,000 due in 24 months, cash price ₹1,00,000. Interest income over the period (₹)?
Advance ₹4,000 two years before delivery at 6%. Revenue at delivery (₹)?
₹800 a month for 24 months with a ₹2,000 port-in credit. Transaction price (₹)?
recall.why: 19,200 − 2,000 (SM Illustration 53).

twist.q: The contract rate is 10% but the customer would borrow at 14%. Which rate sets revenue?
twist.a: 14% — the rate of a separate financing transaction; revenue = PV of the instalments at 14% (₹91,31,346 in SM Illustration 39).

levels.title: Step 4 — allocation, discounts and variable consideration
levels.hook: Allocation tables earn easy marks if the SSP order and the para 82 test are right.

teach.html: Observable price first; else adjusted market assessment, expected cost plus margin, or residual (only if highly variable or uncertain).
Spread proportionately unless the entity regularly sells a bundle at that discount (para 82) — then the discount goes to that bundle, before any residual estimate.
Allocate variable consideration entirely to one obligation only if it relates to that obligation and the result is consistent with the objective. Later changes follow the inception basis.

recall.q: X ₹50,000, Y ₹25,000, Z ₹45,000; Y+Z regularly ₹50,000; all three sold for ₹1,00,000, Y and Z delivered at different times. Allocated to Y (₹)?
recall.why: 50,000 × 25,000 ÷ 70,000 (SM Illustration 55 Case A).

recall.q: The residual approach can be used whenever a stand-alone selling price is not observable.
recall.why: Only if the price is highly variable or uncertain; then check the result is within the observed range.

recall.q: ₹20 lakh bonus becomes highly probable for software implementation (allocated ₹1 crore), now 60% complete. Cumulative revenue for that obligation (₹ lakh)?
recall.why: 60% × ₹120 lakh (SM Illustration 57).

twist.q: With Product Alpha added and a total price of ₹1,05,000, the residual for Alpha is ₹5,000 against a range of ₹15,000–₹45,000. What now?
twist.a: Residual is not faithful; estimate Alpha's SSP by another method and allocate ₹1,05,000 on relative SSPs.

levels.title: Step 5 — over time or point in time, progress, repurchase, bill-and-hold, licences
levels.hook: Bill-and-hold and licence nature appear repeatedly, almost verbatim from the SM.

teach.html: (a) customer consumes as you perform; (b) customer controls the asset as it is built; (c) no alternative use and an enforceable right to payment (cost + reasonable margin) for work to date.
Single method; exclude inputs that do not show progress; uninstalled materials at zero margin outside the percentage.

Repurchase: call/forward below price = lease, at/above = financing; put depends on economic incentive. Bill-and-hold needs a substantive reason, separate identification, readiness and no ability to redirect, plus custodial service. Licence: access (over time) only if the entity's activities significantly affect the IP and expose the customer and are not separate goods.

levels.picture:
FactAnswer
Specialised satellite, right to cost + margin on terminationOver time (35c)
Only keeps payments received on terminationPoint in time
Sale ₹1 million, call at ₹1.1 millionFinancing
Sale ₹10,00,000, put at ₹9,00,000, market ₹7,50,000Lease
1975 symphony recordingRight to use
Sports team name while the team playsRight to access

recall.q: Transaction price ₹50 lakh; elevators ₹15 lakh delivered early; other costs ₹5 lakh of ₹25 lakh incurred. Revenue (₹ lakh)?
recall.why: 20% × 35 + 15 = 22 (SM Illustration 65).

recall.q: Which is NOT a bill-and-hold criterion?
opts: Product separately identified as the customer's
Entity cannot use or redirect the product
recall.why: Payment is not one of the four criteria; readiness for physical transfer is.

recall.q: A franchise where the franchisor must keep maintaining the brand gives a right to use, recognised at a point in time.
recall.why: It is a right to access — up-front fee recognised over the franchise period (SM PQ 4).

twist.q: In the put option case the expected market price rises to ₹9,50,000 (above the ₹9,00,000 put price). What changes?
twist.a: No significant economic incentive to exercise → account as a sale with a right of return, not a lease.

levels.title: Contract costs, presentation and service concessions
levels.hook: SCA carried 10 marks in Nov 2022; contract costs are a quick theory MCQ.

teach.html: Capitalise incremental costs to obtain (commission on signing) if recoverable; expense if amortisation ≤ 1 year. Capitalise fulfilment costs outside other standards only if direct, resource-generating and recoverable. Amortise over the expected period including renewals.
Paid first → contract liability. Performed first: conditional right → contract asset; only time left → receivable.
Infrastructure is not the operator's PPE. Guaranteed cash from the grantor → financial asset; right to collect tolls → intangible asset. Borrowing costs capitalised only in the intangible model.

recall.q: Which cost is capitalised as a cost to obtain a contract?
recall.why: Only the commission is incremental (SM 10.1).

recall.q: Five-year contract renewable yearly to 10; customers stay 7 years on average. Amortisation period (years)?
recall.why: Initial term plus expected renewals (SM Illustration 74).

recall.q: Government guarantees ₹200 crore to the toll-road operator. The operator recognises…
recall.why: Unconditional right to cash → financial asset (SM Illustration 75(I)).

twist.q: The operator instead collects tolls from road users with no guarantee. What changes in the accounts?
twist.a: Intangible asset model: Dr Intangible asset / Cr Revenue at the fair value of construction; amortise over the operation period; borrowing costs capitalised during construction.

compare.title: Licence of IP: right to access vs right to use

rows.a: The IP as it exists throughout the licence period
rows.b: The IP as it exists when the licence is granted

rows.a: Required or reasonably expected, and significantly affect the IP
rows.b: None that significantly affect the IP (IP is static or has stand-alone functionality)

rows.a: Exposed to the positive or negative effects of those activities
rows.b: Not exposed — benefit does not depend on the entity

rows.a: No — they do not transfer anything separately
rows.b: If they are (e.g. distinct upgrades) they are ignored in judging the licence

rows.a: Over time, across the licence period
rows.b: At the point the customer can use and benefit from the IP

rows.a: Chhota Bheem character licence; sports team name while playing; franchise with brand maintenance
rows.b: 1975 symphony recording; completed film; software with when-and-if-available upgrades; dormant brand from a brand collector

rows.a: Recognised when the later of sale/usage and satisfaction occurs
rows.b: Recognised when the later of sale/usage and satisfaction occurs

sorter.s: Franchisor must keep maintaining the brand through marketing and product improvements.
sorter.why: Activities significantly affect the IP and expose the franchisee (SM PQ 4).

sorter.s: Licence of a 1975 classical recording for use in advertisements.
sorter.why: Significant stand-alone functionality; no obligation to change it (SM Illustration 69).

sorter.s: Film studio will market a completed film heavily.
sorter.why: Marketing does not change the film's form or functionality (SM Illustration 71).

sorter.s: Team name and logo licensed while the team keeps playing games.
sorter.why: Value depends on the team's ongoing activities (SM Illustration 72(i)).

sorter.s: Revenue from a sales-based royalty waits for the customer's sales.
sorter.why: The royalty exception applies to both kinds of licence.

sorter.s: Payment is made monthly over two years, so revenue must be over time.
sorter.why: Payment terms do not decide the nature of the licence (SM Illustration 69 is paid monthly but is a right to use).

solves.title: Material right: discount voucher
solves.tip: Only the extra discount counts. Spend × extra % × chance = the voucher's price; then split the sale in the ratio of the two prices.

variants.label: Base case (SM Illustration 23)
variants.q: Product A sold for ₹1,000 with a 40% voucher on up to ₹1,000 of purchases in 30 days. Everyone gets 10% in that period anyway. 80% of customers will use it, spending ₹500 on average.

steps.ask: Stand-alone selling price of the voucher (₹).

variants.label: Twist: PYQ May 2025 MCQ 13
variants.q: Product H sold for ₹2,000 with a 40% voucher; 10% seasonal discount for all; 90% likely to be used on ₹1,000 of purchases.

variants.label: Twist: everyone gets 40%
variants.q: Same as the base case, but the seasonal discount for all customers is 40%.

steps.ask: Is the voucher a separate performance obligation?
opts: No — it is a marketing offer, no allocation
steps.say: No incremental discount → no material right.

solves.title: Contract modification: cumulative catch-up
solves.tip: Blend the rate first: (old total + added) ÷ new hours. Then re-price what is done and compare with what is booked.

variants.label: Base case (SM Illustration 9)
variants.q: 200 hours at ₹150. After 100 hours, 50 more hours are added at ₹100. Remaining work is not distinct.

variants.label: Twist: PYQ May 2026 MCQ 12
variants.q: 200 hours at ₹300; after 100 hours, 50 hours more at ₹200.

variants.label: Twist: SM PQ 8 (bonus becomes includable)
variants.q: Price ₹20,00,000 (bonus ₹2,50,000 constrained); costs ₹11,00,000; 65% done in year 1. Modification adds ₹1,50,000 price and ₹80,000 cost and makes the bonus highly probable. Cost to date ₹7,15,000.

solves.title: Sale with a right of return
solves.tip: Three numbers, three multiplications: price × kept, price × returned, cost × returned.

variants.label: Base case (SM Illustration 34)
variants.q: 1,000 products at ₹50, cost ₹30, 30-day return right; 970 expected to be kept; recovery costs immaterial.

steps.ask: Asset for goods to be recovered (₹).

variants.label: Twist: restocking fee (SM Example 4)
variants.q: 10 units at ₹100, 10% expected returns, 3% restocking fee charged on returns.

variants.label: Twist: no experience of returns
variants.q: New product, 90-day return right, no evidence of returns (as in SM Illustration 38).

opts: Possibly none until the return period ends — the constraint applies
steps.say: Without experience the estimate may be fully constrained.

solves.title: Input method with uninstalled materials
solves.tip: Take the bought-in item out of both the price and the costs, find the %, then add the item back at cost.

variants.label: Base case (SM Illustration 65)
variants.q: Price ₹50,00,000; elevators ₹15,00,000 (delivered early, procured); other costs ₹25,00,000, of which ₹5,00,000 incurred.

variants.label: Twist: SM TYK 3
variants.q: Price ₹50,00,000; air conditioners ₹10,00,000; other costs ₹30,00,000, of which ₹6,00,000 incurred.

variants.label: Twist: PYQ Nov 2024 MCQ 5
variants.q: Price ₹30,00,000; elevator ₹10,00,000; other costs ₹12,00,000, of which ₹3,00,000 incurred.

solves.title: Significant financing component
solves.tip: Arrears: divide by (1 + r)ⁿ to get revenue. Advance: multiply by (1 + r)ⁿ to get revenue.

variants.label: Base case (SM Illustration 38)
variants.q: ₹1,21,000 payable 24 months after delivery; implicit rate 10%; cash price ₹1,00,000.

variants.label: Twist: advance (SM Illustration 40)
variants.q: ₹4,000 received two years before delivery; incremental borrowing rate 6%.

solves.title: Loyalty points: allocate and release
solves.tip: Points value = points × value × expected redemption. Share the sale in the ratio sale : points value.

variants.label: Base case (SM PQ 5(a))
variants.q: Sales ₹10,00,000; 10 points per ₹500; ₹0.50 a point; 80% expected to be redeemed.

variants.q: ₹10,000 stay earns 100 points with a stand-alone selling price of ₹500.

hooks.story: A 40% coupon is worth only 30% if everyone gets 10% anyway — and only if they use it.
The elevator is lifted out of the percentage and shifted into revenue at cost.

hooks.h: Buy back cheap = rent; buy back dear = loan
hooks.story: Sell at 10, buy back at 9 → you rented it out; buy back at 11 → you borrowed 10 and paid 1 interest.

links.how: Assurance → Ind AS 37 provision; service (sold separately or beyond assurance) → performance obligation and contract liability.
Consignee never controls the goods; a buyer with a return right does.
Only a discount beyond what others get is a performance obligation.
Conditional on more performance vs only time left.
Estimate first (EV or most likely), then include only the highly probable part.
Catch-up re-runs the progress calculation with the new price.
Interest on the receivable or contract liability is measured under Ind AS 109.
A forward or call below the original price is a lease; a put with significant incentive likewise.
RTP May 2024 Q12 and RTP Nov 2026 Q11 test revenue timing inside an ethics case.
Toll licence is an intangible; borrowing costs capitalised during construction.
Both release a deferred amount by cumulative proportion minus what was released earlier.
